summary: Discovery call focused on reliability, incident tolerance, and fallback strategies across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployment options. Arcadia is evaluating Redwood for mission-critical route-planning and manifest generation with strict SLOs; primary concerns were multi-region failover, predictable latency under load, fallbacks to cheaper model variants, and SOC2/KMS integration for Private deployments.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Priya Shah: Good, thanks. We tried to keep the agenda tight: reliability, incident tolerance, fallback policy questions, and a bit about deployment modes.
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: Great, we'll jump right in. Quick context check — you're running route-planning at Arcadia, low-latency H100 pools now, and looking at inference to power ETA and manifest summaries?
[00:28] Ravi Kapoor: That's right. We're doing near-real-time route updates; 99th percentile latency targets are 250ms for live features.
[00:36] Carlos Mendes: And we have bursty traffic — weekdays mornings heavy, but also spikes when a region's UPS flaps. We need graceful degradation not to kill user experience.
[00:48] Maya Chen: Understood. Just to frame options: Redwood Hosted gives fastest onboarding, Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and SLAs, Private gives VPC/on-prem for compliance. We're trying to map policies like multi-region routing and fallbacks to those modes.
[01:02] Priya Shah: A few quick questions: if an entire region goes down, what's the typical failover time? And do you do automatic model variant fallback if the primary model is out of capacity?
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: Good ones. For Hosted we have automated routing across regions with health checks. Failover detection window depends on your health-check cadence but typically you see traffic shift within 30-90 seconds. For Dedicated, with reserved capacity we can do instant routing within seconds if you've got cross-region peering and reserved pools in both regions.
[01:30] Jordan Blake: When you say health checks, are those application-level or infra-level? We need auditable events for incident post-mortem.
[01:36] Liam O'Connor: Both. We emit metrics and events to the console and can stream to your observability (Datadog/Splunk) via tracing hooks and webhooks. All failover decisions are logged; we also provide audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM.
[01:48] Anika Rao: What about model fallbacks — for example, if the high-capacity gpt-xx-8k model is overloaded, can you fallback to a quantized variant, or even to a local cached response?
[01:58] Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood supports policy-based fallbacks. You can define a chain: primary model -> quantized variant -> cached prefix -> simpler smaller model. We surface metrics on quality drift and token-cost delta so you can set thresholds.
[02:10] Priya Shah: How do you measure quality drift automatically? We run a set of prompts/benchmarks nightly.
[02:16] Liam O'Connor: We integrate with your eval sets. On Dedicated we can run shadow traffic and emit regression alerts if quality drops beyond configured thresholds. For Hosted we offer a managed eval pipeline and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[02:30] Ravi Kapoor: What's your guaranteed SLA for Dedicated? We have strict uptime requirements in our contracts with carriers.
[02:36] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we offer a 99.95% uptime SLA for the serving control plane and configurable p95/p99 latency SLOs depending on the commit level. The SLA language and credits are in the one-pager I'll send. Hosted SLA is lower but typically fast for small teams.
[02:52] Carlos Mendes: And on the Private option, if we run an on-prem appliance, do you still support automatic multi-region routing?
[02:59] Liam O'Connor: For Private deployments, multi-region routing is customer-controlled — Redwood's control plane can coordinate if you opt into our hybrid control plane. Alternatively, you can run independent Private regions and route via your global load balancer. There are tradeoffs on observability centralization and cross-region KV cache sharing.
[03:15] Priya Shah: KV cache sharing — we use heavy prefix reuse for manifest expansions; if we don't share KV caches, latency increases.
[03:22] Liam O'Connor: Right. Hosted and Dedicated have built-in cache coherency across colocated pools. For Private, we support a KV cache replication option but it adds network overhead and eventual consistency windows — typically tens to low hundreds of milliseconds for propagation depending on region distance.
[03:38] Jordan Blake: Encryption — we need to ensure keys are customer-managed. How does KMS integration work across modes?
[03:44] Maya Chen: We support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Dedicated and Private. Hosted can support BYOK for enterprise customers via a managed HSM in the region. We'll include a diagram in the docs.
[03:55] Anika Rao: Can you speak to incident tolerance examples — like a rolling kernel update that takes down a node pool — what does Redwood do to maintain SLOs?
[04:03] Liam O'Connor: We do graceful draining of nodes, continuous batching re-routing, and automatic traffic rebalancing. For Dedicated, your reserved pool cushions the effect; for Hosted we have pre-warmed fallbacks and the ability to spin up burst nodes in other regions, but that can add a setup time of 1-3 minutes depending on instance availability.
[04:20] Priya Shah: We care a lot about tail latency. If a fallback model is used, do you surface the change in latency and confidence so our product can show degraded mode?
[04:29] Maya Chen: Absolutely — every request is annotated with route metadata, model variant used, latency, and a confidence/quality score if you enable eval tracking. You can use that to show degraded UI or to trigger alerts.
[04:40] Carlos Mendes: How easy is it to write routing policies? Can we define percent-based rollouts or conditional rules by region and tenant?
[04:47] Liam O'Connor: Yes. The console and API let you define rollout policies: percentage rollouts, canaries by tenant, time-based overrides, and conditional rules by region, cost, or latency. Policies are declarative YAML, and we can share templates.
[05:00] Ravi Kapoor: On cost — there's always a tension between having dedicated capacity everywhere and just routing to other regions. Can you help us model the cost/latency trade-offs?
[05:08] Maya Chen: That's part of Redwood Optimize — we can run a quick estimate based on your traffic percentiles and suggested batch sizes to show cost delta between Hosted, Dedicated, and hybrid. I'll include a sample calc with the pricing doc.
[05:20] Priya Shah: From a compliance view, we need audit trails and retention. What's retention for logs and transcripts?
[05:26] Maya Chen: Audit logs retention is configurable as an add-on; typical defaults are 90 days, with enterprise tiers allowing longer retention at extra cost. We can also stream logs to your S3 for long-term storage.
[05:36] Jordan Blake: Any customers similar to us — logistics with strict latency?
[05:39] Maya Chen: We have a few references in transport/logistics — I can share a short case study (link) and an anonymized latency/availability spreadsheet.
[05:48] Carlos Mendes: Ok, some nitty gritty: if a model variant is unavailable due to a quantization mismatch or missing kernels on GPU, does Redwood automatically choose a compatible variant?
[05:58] Liam O'Connor: The runtime has a compatibility matrix. If a kernel mismatch occurs, it can route to a compatible quantized or CPU-backed fallback. We also log the reason. Sometimes the names get fuzzy in transcripts — our console flags model compatibility and suggests repro steps.
[06:12] Priya Shah: Do you do chaos testing with customers to validate failover?
[06:16] Liam O'Connor: We run internal chaos tests and can coordinate customer-facing failover drills during POC. We can also run shadow traffic and simulate regional outages for validation.
[06:26] Ravi Kapoor: For the POC, we'd want a weekly cadence check and a final stress test. Timeline is Q3 production — ideally Sept go-live.
[06:33] Maya Chen: That fits a typical cadence. For POC we'd propose a 6-week engagement: week 1 onboarding, weeks 2-4 integration + stress tests, week 5 tuning, week 6 handover.
[06:46] Carlos Mendes: On SSO and roles — can we enforce per-route RBAC?
[06:50] Liam O'Connor: Yes — RBAC is available in Console. For Private you can tie into your IdP and enforce route-level permissions and token scopes.
[06:58] Jordan Blake: What's involved in the legal negotiation for Dedicated SLA credits?
[07:02] Maya Chen: Standard contract negotiation. We have template SOWs and SLA language; credits are a percentage payout depending on downtime windows. I'll send a redlineable copy.
[07:12] Priya Shah: Any gotchas we should know about for on-prem? Networking for KV cache replication and latency are the main concerns?
[07:18] Liam O'Connor: Yes. Network egress and latency for cache replication are the two big tradeoffs. Also orchestration of GPU drivers and kernel versions in on-prem stacks can lead to occasional incompatibilities; we provide a compatibility matrix and pre-tested images.
[07:34] Ravi Kapoor: Let's talk about observability integration — can we get per-token traces exported?
[07:40] Liam O'Connor: We provide per-request traces and token-level timing metrics; we can stream to your tracing backend and attach logs for post-mortem.
[07:48] Maya Chen: Quick recap — next steps: we'll send pricing/SLA, multi-region routing docs, SOC2/arch diagrams, schedule SE deep dive with SREs on July 1st. Customer to share traffic patterns and infra diagrams. Any other asks?
[07:58] Priya Shah: Please include sample routing YAML and an example policy that falls back to a cached summary if latency above threshold.
[08:06] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and set the calendar for the deep dive.
[08:12] Ravi Kapoor: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:15] [call ends]
